questionText: Man facing north turns 135° left, then 225° right. Facing?
hints: This is a turning problem. A left turn and a right turn undo each other, so think about the turn that is left over.
The right turn is bigger than the left turn. Find how many degrees of right turn remain after the left turn is cancelled.
Similar example: a girl faces north, turns 45° left and then 225° right. The turns leave 225° − 45° = 180° to the right. Half a turn from north is south, so she faces south.

stepByStep.text: Turning left and then right cancel each other. The right turn is bigger.
So the man ends up turned 90° to the right from north.
A quarter turn to the right from north points east. He is facing East.

misconceptions.A: This is where he faces after the first turn only. He still has to turn 225° to the right.
misconceptions.B: This would be a turn of 135° to the right from north. The turn left over is 225° − 135° = 90° to the right.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The turns leave 90° to the right, and a quarter turn right from north is east.
misconceptions.D: North-West is on the left side of north. The bigger turn is to the right, so he ends on the right side.

questionText: Angle = 35°. Sum of complementary and supplementary?
hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 35° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 20°, the complement is 90° − 20° = 70° and the supplement is 180° − 20° = 160°. Their sum is 70° + 160° = 230°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 200°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The complement is 55°, the supplement is 145°, and 55° + 145° = 200°.
misconceptions.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 35° = 55° and 180° − 35° = 145°. Then add them.
misconceptions.C: This is 145° + 35°, the supplement plus the angle itself. Add the complement and the supplement instead.
misconceptions.D: Find both angles first: the complement is 55° and the supplement is 145°. Then add the two.

questionText: Angle = (1/5)th of supplementary. Find angle.
hints: This is a supplementary angle problem with parts. The angle and its supplement together make 180°.
If the angle is 1 part, its supplement is 5 equal parts. Count how many parts make 180° altogether.
Similar example: an angle is one third of its supplement. The angle is 1 part and the supplement is 3 parts, so 4 parts make 180°. One part is 180° ÷ 4 = 45°. The angle is 45°.

stepByStep.text: The angle is one fifth of its supplement. So if the angle is 1 part, the supplement is 5 parts.
Together they make 180°, and that is 6 parts.
Find one part.
Check: the supplement is 150°, and one fifth of 150° is 30°. The angle is 30°.

misconceptions.A: Check it: the supplement of 40° is 140°, and one fifth of 140° is 28°, not 40°.
misconceptions.B: Check it: the supplement of 35° is 145°, and one fifth of 145° is 29°, not 35°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 30° and 150° make 180°, and 30° is one fifth of 150°.
misconceptions.D: Check it: the supplement of 50° is 130°, and one fifth of 130° is 26°, not 50°.

questionText: Supplementary angle of obtuse angle is always?
hints: This is about types of angles. Think about how big an obtuse angle is and what its supplement must add to it.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. Its supplement is what is left to reach 180°. Is that more or less than 90°?

Similar example: what kind of angle is the supplement of an acute angle? Try 40°: its supplement is 180° − 40° = 140°. An acute angle is less than 90°, so what is left is always more than 90°. The supplement of an acute angle is always obtuse.

stepByStep.text: An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°.
Its supplement is 180° take away the angle. Taking away more than 90° leaves less than 90°.
For example, the supplement of 110° is 70°.
An angle less than 90° is acute. So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always an Acute Angle.

misconceptions.A: The supplement would be a right angle only if the angle itself were 90°. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Complementary describes two angles that add up to 90°. Here, ask how big the supplement is.
misconceptions.C: A straight angle is 180° all by itself. The supplement is only the part left over after the obtuse angle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Taking more than 90° away from 180° always leaves less than 90°, which is an acute angle.

questionText: Sum of complementary and supplementary of 48°?
hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 48° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 30°, the complement is 90° − 30° = 60° and the supplement is 180° − 30° = 150°. Their sum is 60° + 150° = 210°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.
misconceptions.C: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too much. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.

questionText: Sum of complementary and supplementary angles of 48°?
hints: This question has two parts. Find the complementary angle and the supplementary angle of the same angle, then add them.
The complement of 48° is what must be added to 48° to make 90°. Find it first, then find the supplement in the same way with 180°.
Similar example: for an angle of 25°, the complement is 90° − 25° = 65° and the supplement is 180° − 25° = 155°. Their sum is 65° + 155° = 220°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
misconceptions.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
misconceptions.C: Find both angles first: the complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Then add the two.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.

questionText: Angle between hour and minute hand at 7:20 pm?
hints: This is a clock angle problem. The clock face has 12 equal gaps between the numbers, and the hour hand keeps moving slowly as the minutes pass.
A full turn is 360°, so each gap between two numbers is 30°. At 20 minutes the minute hand points at 4. Now think about where the hour hand is: it has moved past 7.
Similar example: at 3:30 the minute hand is at 6. The hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so it is 15° before 4. From 4 to 6 is 2 gaps, which is 60°. The angle is 60° + 15° = 75°.

stepByStep.text: Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30°.
At 20 minutes past, the minute hand points at 4. From 4 to 7 is 3 gaps.
20 minutes is one third of an hour, so the hour hand has moved one third of a gap past 7.
Add the two parts.
The angle between the hands is 100°.

misconceptions.A: This is the angle from 4 to 7. The hour hand has moved a little past 7 in 20 minutes, so add that bit.
misconceptions.B: This adds too much for the hour hand. In 20 minutes it moves one third of a 30° gap, which is 10°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! From 4 to 7 is 90°, and the hour hand is 10° past 7, so the angle is 100°.
misconceptions.D: Count the gaps from 4 to 7 first: 3 gaps of 30°. Then add the small bit the hour hand has moved past 7.

questionText: Man walking south-west turns clockwise to face north. Degrees turned?
hints: This is a turning problem on the compass. Between two neighbouring directions, such as north and north-east, the turn is 45°.
Start at south-west and move clockwise. Name each direction you pass until you reach north, and count the 45° steps.

Similar example: a boy faces north-east and turns clockwise to face north-west. He passes east, south-east, south, south-west, west and then north-west. That is 6 steps of 45°, so he turns 6 × 45° = 270°.

stepByStep.text: The eight compass directions are 45° apart.
Clockwise from south-west he passes west, then north-west, then north. That is 3 steps.
Each step is 45°.
135° is not in the list, so the answer is None of these.

misconceptions.A: 90° clockwise from south-west reaches north-west. He has to go one more step to reach north.
misconceptions.B: 225° is the turn the other way round, anticlockwise. Clockwise it is shorter.
misconceptions.C: A turn of 180° from south-west ends at north-east, the opposite direction.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The turn is 3 steps of 45°, which is 135°, and that is not one of the listed values.

questionText: Angle between hour and minute at 18 minutes past 5?
hints: This is a clock angle problem. Measure each hand's turn from the 12, and remember the hour hand keeps moving as the minutes pass.
The minute hand turns 6° every minute. Find how far it has turned from 12 in 18 minutes. Then find where the hour hand is.

Similar example: at 10 minutes past 4, the minute hand has turned 10 × 6° = 60° from 12. The hour hand has turned 4 × 30° = 120°, plus 5° more for the 10 minutes, so it is at 125°. The angle between them is 125° − 60° = 65°.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand turns 6° each minute. In 18 minutes it is 108° from 12.
At 5 o'clock the hour hand is 150° from 12.
The hour hand moves 1° every 2 minutes, so in 18 minutes it moves 9° more.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands.
The angle is 51°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand at 108°, and 159° − 108° = 51°.
misconceptions.B: Check the hour hand. It starts at 150° and moves 9° more in 18 minutes, so it is at 159°. Then subtract 108°.
misconceptions.C: Check the minute hand. It turns 6° each minute, so 18 minutes is 108° from 12.
misconceptions.D: Check the subtraction: the hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand is at 108°.

questionText: Which pair of angles is supplementary?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when they add up to exactly 180°.
Add the two angles in each pair. Start with 62° + 128° and see whether it makes 180°.
Similar example: is 112.5° and 67.5° a supplementary pair? Add them: 112.5 + 67.5 = 180. Yes, they are supplementary. Is 95° and 75°? 95 + 75 = 170, so that pair is not.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°, so add each pair.
Add the first pair.
Add the second pair.
Add the third pair.
Add the fourth pair.
Only the last pair makes 180°. The supplementary pair is 140.5° & 39.5°.

misconceptions.B: 73.5° + 107.5° = 181°. That is just 1° too much.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 140.5° + 39.5° = 180°, so this pair is supplementary.

questionText: A line segment has how many end points?
hints: This is about the parts of a line. Think about the difference between a line, a ray and a line segment.
A line segment is a piece of a line that starts at one point and stops at another. Count the points where it stops.
Similar example: how many end points does a ray have? A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. So a ray has 1 end point.

stepByStep.text: A line segment is a straight path between two points.
It stops at both of those points, so each one is an end point.
A line segment has 2 end points.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A line segment stops at both sides, so it has 2 end points.
misconceptions.B: One end point describes a ray, which goes on forever on one side. A line segment stops at both sides.
misconceptions.C: No end points describes a line, which goes on forever both ways. A line segment stops at both sides.
misconceptions.D: A line segment has endless points on it, but it only stops at its two ends.

questionText: How many lines can pass through two distinct points?
hints: This is about lines and points. Picture two dots on paper and a ruler.
Mark two different points and lay a ruler so its edge touches both. Try to draw a second, different straight line through both.
Similar example: how many lines can pass through a single point? You can keep turning a ruler around that point and draw a new line each time. So endless lines pass through a single point.

stepByStep.text: Mark two different points and join them with a ruler. You get a straight line.
Any other straight line through both points lies exactly on top of the first.
So only One line can pass through two distinct points.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Two points fix the line completely, so there is exactly one.
misconceptions.B: Try drawing a second straight line through both points. It falls exactly on the first one.
misconceptions.C: Endless lines pass through a single point. Once a second point is fixed, the line cannot turn any more.
misconceptions.D: You can always join two points with a ruler, so there is a line.

questionText: Three or more points on the same line are called:
hints: This is a geometry word question. Think about what the parts of each word mean.
'Co' means together, as in co-operate. Look for the word that means together on one line.
Similar example: three or more lines that pass through the same point are called concurrent lines. The word tells you they run together through one point.

stepByStep.text: 'Co' means together and 'linear' means on a line.
So points that lie together on the same line are called collinear points.
Three or more points on the same line are called Collinear.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Collinear means lying together on the same line.
misconceptions.B: Non-collinear means the points do not all lie on one line. Here they do.
misconceptions.C: Concurrent is used for lines that meet at one point. Here we are naming points on one line.
misconceptions.D: Parallel is used for lines that never meet. Here we are naming points on one line.

questionText: An angle less than 90° is called:
hints: This is about naming angles by size. Each name goes with a range of degrees, measured against 90° and 180°.
Compare with a right angle, which is exactly 90°. Which name is used for an angle smaller than that?
Similar example: an angle more than 90° but less than 180° is called an obtuse angle. For example, 120° is obtuse.

stepByStep.text: A right angle is exactly 90°.
An angle smaller than a right angle, between 0° and 90°, has its own name.
An angle less than 90° is called an Acute angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Acute angles are the ones smaller than 90°.
misconceptions.B: A right angle is exactly 90°, not less.
misconceptions.C: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Here the angle is less than 90°.
misconceptions.D: A straight angle is 180°, a straight line. Here the angle is less than 90°.

questionText: A right angle measures:
hints: This is about the size of a special angle. Think of the corner of a square or of your book.
A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter of a full turn.
Similar example: a straight angle is half of a full turn. Half of 360° is 360° ÷ 2 = 180°, so a straight angle measures 180°.

stepByStep.text: A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a square.
Divide the full turn into 4 equal parts.
A right angle measures 90°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
misconceptions.B: 180° is a straight angle, which is two right angles together.
misconceptions.C: 45° is half of a right angle.
misconceptions.D: 360° is a full turn, which is four right angles.

questionText: An angle of 180° is called a:
hints: This is about naming angles by size. Picture what the two arms of the angle look like.
Draw an angle of 180°. The two arms point in opposite directions. What shape do they make together?
Similar example: an angle of 360° is a full turn back to the start, so it is called a complete angle.

stepByStep.text: 180° is half of a full turn.
The two arms point in opposite directions and form a straight line.
So an angle of 180° is called a Straight angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! At 180° the two arms form a straight line.
misconceptions.B: A right angle is 90°, half of 180°.
misconceptions.C: A reflex angle is more than 180° and less than 360°.
misconceptions.D: A complete angle is a full turn of 360°.

questionText: What type of angle is 135°?
hints: This is about naming an angle by its size. Compare the angle with 90° and with 180°.
Is 135° more than 90°? Is it less than 180°? Use both answers to pick the name.
Similar example: what type of angle is 200°? It is more than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle.

stepByStep.text: 135° is more than 90°, so it is bigger than a right angle.
135° is less than 180°, so it is smaller than a straight angle.
An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse. So 135° is an Obtuse angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 135° lies between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
misconceptions.B: An acute angle is less than 90°. 135° is more than 90°.
misconceptions.C: A right angle is exactly 90°. 135° is bigger.
misconceptions.D: A reflex angle is more than 180°. 135° is less than 180°.

questionText: Two angles that add up to 90° are called:
hints: This is a geometry word question about pairs of angles. Two special totals have their own names: 90° and 180°.
One name is for pairs that make a right angle, the other for pairs that make a straight line. Decide which total 90° is.
Similar example: 110° and 70° add up to 180°. Two angles that add up to 180° are called supplementary angles.

stepByStep.text: Two angles that add up to 90° make a right angle together.
For example, 30° and 60°.
Such a pair of angles is called Complementary.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Angles that add up to 90° are complementary.
misconceptions.B: Supplementary angles add up to 180°. A total of 90° has a different name.
misconceptions.C: Adjacent angles sit next to each other and share an arm. They can add up to any total.
misconceptions.D: Vertically opposite angles are formed where two lines cross, and they are equal. The name for a total of 90° is different.

questionText: Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
hints: Angles that lie side by side on a straight line add up to a straight angle. Remember how many degrees that is.
A straight angle is 180°. Add the two angles you know, then see what is left.
A similar one: two angles of 50° and 70° on a straight line make 120° together, so the third angle is 180° − 120° = 60°.

stepByStep.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles.
Take this away from 180°.
The third angle is 65°.

misconceptions.A: 115° is the two known angles added together. Take that away from 180° to find the third.
misconceptions.C: 245° comes from using 360°. That is for angles all the way around a point. On a straight line the total is 180°.
misconceptions.D: 75° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 115 + 65 = 180.

questionText: A round pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices. Ria eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the remaining slices make together?
hints: The angles all the way around a point add up to 360°. Equal slices share this equally.
Find the angle of one slice by sharing 360° among 8 slices. Then count the slices that are left.
A similar one: a cake cut into 6 equal slices has 360° ÷ 6 = 60° in each slice. If 2 are eaten, the 4 left make 4 × 60° = 240°.

stepByStep.text: The angle at the centre of one slice.
Slices left.
Angle made by the slices left.
The remaining slices make an angle of 225°.

misconceptions.A: 135° is the angle of the 3 slices Ria ate. The question asks about the slices that are left.
misconceptions.B: 45° is the angle of one slice. Five slices are left.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Five slices of 45° each make 225°.
misconceptions.D: 315° is what is left after only one slice is eaten. Ria ate 3 slices.

questionText: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn between 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. on the same day?
hints: The hour hand goes once around the clock, 360°, in 12 hours. Find how far it turns in one hour.
In one hour the hour hand turns 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. How many hours are there from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.?
A similar one: from 1 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. is 2 and a half hours. The hour hand turns 30° + 30° for the two hours and 15° for the half hour, which is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand turns 30° every hour.
From 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.
Four hours give 120°, and half an hour gives half of 30°, which is 15°.
The hour hand turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 120° for the four hours and 15° more for the half hour make 135°.
misconceptions.B: 120° is the turn for 4 hours. The hour hand keeps moving during the extra half hour.
misconceptions.C: 270° uses 60° for each hour. The hour hand moves only 30° in an hour.
misconceptions.D: 150° is the turn for 5 full hours. The time from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.

questionText: Arjun is facing East. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: A quarter turn is 90° and takes you from one main direction to the next. Anticlockwise is the opposite way to the hands of a clock.
Starting from East, one quarter turn anticlockwise brings Arjun to North. Make two more quarter turns the same way.
A similar one: facing North, a half turn anticlockwise goes North to West to South. So that person ends up facing South.

stepByStep.text: Going anticlockwise, the directions come in the order East, North, West, South.
First quarter turn: East to North. Second quarter turn: North to West.
Third quarter turn: West to South.
Arjun is now facing South.

misconceptions.A: North is where Arjun faces after one quarter turn. He makes three quarter turns.
misconceptions.B: West is where Arjun faces after a half turn. One more quarter turn is still to come.
misconceptions.C: He would face East again only after a full turn. Three quarters is one quarter short of that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! East to North to West to South is three quarter turns anticlockwise.

questionText: A ladder leans against an upright wall on level ground. The ladder makes an angle of 58° with the ground. What angle does the ladder make with the wall?
hints: The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle. An upright wall meets level ground at a right angle.
One angle of the triangle is 90°, so the other two angles together make 90°. One of them is 58°.
A similar one: a ladder that makes 65° with the ground makes 90° − 65° = 25° with the wall.

stepByStep.text: The wall and the ground meet at 90°. The three angles of the triangle add up to 180°.
So the two angles at the ends of the ladder add up to 90°.
Take away the angle with the ground.
The ladder makes an angle of 32° with the wall.

misconceptions.A: 122° comes from taking 58° from 180°. The right angle between the wall and the ground uses up 90° of that.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 58° and 32° make 90° together, and the third angle is the right angle.
misconceptions.C: 42° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 58 + 32 = 90.
misconceptions.D: 58° is the angle with the ground. The two angles would be equal only if each were 45°.

questionText: At 6:00 the hands of a clock make an angle of 180°. By how many degrees has the angle between the hands become smaller at 6:30?
hints: Both hands move. In half an hour the minute hand goes halfway around, and the hour hand moves a little too.
At 6:30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand is not at 6 any more: it is halfway between 6 and 7. How many degrees is half of one hour space?
A similar one: at 3:00 the angle is 90°. At 3:30 the minute hand is at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so the angle is 90° − 15° = 75°. The angle became smaller by 15°.

stepByStep.text: At 6:30 the minute hand points exactly at 6.
The hour hand has moved halfway from 6 to 7. One hour space is 30°, so half of it is 15°.
So the angle between the hands at 6:30 is 15°.
Compare with the angle at 6:00.
The angle has become smaller by 165°.

misconceptions.A: 180° would be right if the hands were together at 6:30. The hour hand has moved on, halfway towards 7.
misconceptions.B: 150° allows a whole hour space of 30° between the hands. In half an hour the hour hand moves only half a space, 15°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angle goes from 180° down to 15°, which is 165° smaller.
misconceptions.D: 15° is the angle between the hands at 6:30. The question asks how much smaller it is than 180°.

questionText: The lamp of a lighthouse turns at a steady speed and makes one full turn every 40 seconds. Through how many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?
hints: One full turn is 360°. Find how many degrees the lamp turns in one second, then in the number of seconds asked.
Share 360° equally among 40 seconds to get the turn in one second.
A similar one: a wheel makes a full turn in 20 seconds, so it turns 360° ÷ 20 = 18° each second. In 5 seconds it turns 5 × 18° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: A full turn is 360°. Find the turn in one second.
Multiply by 15 seconds.
The lamp turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The lamp turns 9° each second, and 15 × 9 = 135.
misconceptions.B: 150° uses 10° for each second. Share 360° among 40 seconds: it is 9° each second.
misconceptions.C: 24° comes from dividing 360° by 15. Divide by 40 first, because the full turn takes 40 seconds.
misconceptions.D: 600 comes from multiplying 15 by 40. In 15 seconds the lamp makes less than half a turn, so the result must be less than 180°.

questionText: The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. What is the angle?
hints: The complement of an angle is what must be added to make 90°. The supplement is what must be added to make 180°. You can test each choice.
The supplement is always 90° more than the complement. If the supplement is 3 times the complement, then that extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
A similar one: the supplement of an angle is 7 times its complement. Try 75°: its supplement is 105° and its complement is 15°, and 105 = 7 × 15. So that angle is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The supplement is 90° more than the complement, because 180° is 90° more than 90°.
The supplement is 3 times the complement, so the extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
The complement is 45°, so find the angle.
Check: the supplement is 135°, which is 3 times 45°. The angle is 45°.

misconceptions.A: For 60° the supplement is 120° and the complement is 30°. That is 4 times, not 3 times.
misconceptions.B: For 30° the supplement is 150° and the complement is 60°. That is less than 3 times.
misconceptions.C: 135° is the supplement of the angle we want. An angle bigger than 90° has no complement at all.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The supplement of 45° is 135° and its complement is 45°, and 135 = 3 × 45.

questionText: Two straight lines cross each other. One of the angles formed is 4 times the angle beside it. What is the largest angle formed?
hints: When two straight lines cross, two angles that are beside each other lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Think of the smaller angle as 1 part and the angle beside it as 4 parts. Together the 5 parts make 180°.
A similar one: if one angle is twice the angle beside it, then 3 parts make 180°. One part is 60°, so the angles are 60° and 120°, and the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.
The angles are 1 part and 4 parts, which is 5 parts in all.
The larger angle is 4 parts.
The largest angle formed is 144°.

misconceptions.A: 36° is the smaller angle. The angle beside it is 4 times as big.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 36° and 144° lie on a straight line and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: 72° shares the whole turn of 360° into 5 parts. The two angles beside each other share 180°.
misconceptions.D: 288° uses 360° for the two angles. Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.

questionText: Five angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn around it. One of them is 80° and the other four are equal. How big is each of the four equal angles?
hints: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°. Take away the angle you know, then share the rest.
Take 80° away from 360°. What is left is shared equally among the four equal angles.
A similar one: four angles fill the turn around a point. One is 60° and the other three are equal. They share 360° − 60° = 300°, so each is 100°.
